items.abstract:
<jats:p>We present a local, lightweight SQL Agent for giving business analysts natural language access to  structured databases. It is built with open-source technologies: LangChain, DuckDB, and  LLaMA3 through Ollama - this project allows analysts to communicate in plain English and  receive related SQL queries and result sets without coding. The project includes a simplified  Streamlit UI, schema-based prompt generation, interactive error management by editing  queries, and out-puts of both SQL queries and results datasets in CSV format.  Unlike cloud offerings, everything runs fully on a local machine thus ensuring privacy, faster  service, and complete control of data workflows. We describe the various pieces of the  architecture, including a DuckDB backend, local LLM-based query generation, and session-state  logic to persist and recover from faults. The agent saves questions asked by the user and the  execution state of those questions for further insight into debugging and improvement.  We demonstrate the usability of this tool for top-N queries, joins, and filters across customer  and sales data sets as defined by the Chinook schema. The paper describes future enrichments  such as, live MySQL/PostgreSQL connections, role-based access to data, and REST API  extensions.  Our goal is to show how a local LLM agent could simplify data access for non-technical users,  with complete transparency, trust, and control of the system. This agent could be a staring  point for organizations looking to modernize how they provide access to analytics using GenAI  while maintaining overall security and governance.</jats:p>
                <jats:p>
                  The complete implementation accompanying this preprint is archived at Zenodo:
                  <jats:ext-link xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink" xlink:href="https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.17581843">https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.17581843</jats:ext-link>
                </jats:p>
title: A Lightweight Local SQL Agent Using LLMs and DuckDB for Business Analytics

items.abstract: <jats:p>Large language models (LLMs) may judge whether information appears credible without necessarily establishing whether it corresponds to external facts. This study investigates this distinction by operationally separating Semantic Truth (ST), defined as the correspondence of textual claims with external states of affairs, from Epistemic Truth (ET), defined as the credibility or justification conveyed by a text through coherence, plausibility, evidential presentation, and consistency. The dataset comprised 274 source texts, including newer BBC and CNN articles, older CNN articles, and historical articles, from which controlled variants differing in factual accuracy and presentation were generated. In Phase 1, a single LLM reliability score remained relatively high even as factual accuracy decreased, with completely fabricated texts still receiving mean scores above 3 on a 1–5 scale. In some cases, the model also assigned high numerical reliability despite identifying substantial factual problems in its written justification. Phase 2 separately evaluated ST and ET across 548 authentic and fabricated observations. ST provided stronger discrimination between authentic and fabricated texts than ET, achieving an overall AUC of 0.801, sensitivity of 0.766, and specificity of 0.810. However, semantic discrimination varied markedly with information familiarity, ranging from near-chance performance for newer CNN articles to nearly perfect discrimination for older and historical material. These findings demonstrate that targeted semantic prompting improves factual discrimination but does not fully separate semantic correspondence from information familiarity, plausibility, and other non-factual textual cues. More broadly, the ST–ET framework exposes a potentially important form of truth inflation: epistemic credibility may remain high as semantic correspondence is progressively degraded through increasing fabrication. This provides a basis for future studies to determine how far epistemic credibility can be sustained or inflated as factual grounding deteriorates, thereby defining and quantifying an LLM’s tolerance for increasingly plausible fabrication.</jats:p>
title: An investigation into LLMs’ abilities in discerning between true and false information

items.abstract: <jats:p>This paper analyzes a multi-task agency framework where the agent exhibits task-specific abilities. It illustrates how incentive contracts account for the agent's task-specific abilities if contractible performance measures do not reflect the agent's multidimensional contribution to firm value. This paper further sheds light on potential ranking criteria for performance measures in multi-task principal-agent relationships. It demonstrates that performance measures in multi-task agencies cannot necessarily be compared by their respective signal-to-noise ratio as in single-task agency relationships. In fact, it is indispensable to take the induced effort distortion and the measure-cost efficiency into consideration - both determined by the agent's task-specific abilities.</jats:p>
title: Task-Specific Abilities in Multi-Task Principal-Agent Relationships

items.abstract: <jats:p>The multiplication of cloud-based enterprise applications has increased the risk of sensitive information leaks including personally identifiable information (PII), safeguarded health information (PHI), and intellectual property (IP). The accuracy, compliance, and safety of conventional data loss prevention (DLP) systems and single agent large language model (LLM) pipelines have weaknesses when used to address leak scenarios. This paper presents a modular multi-agent LLM system to support enterprise data leaks with five role-specific agents, namely Retriever, Risk Classifier, Summarizer, Redactor, and Orchestrator, coordinated via specified protocols. The experiments were done in public corpora including Enron emails and legal texts, and a synthetic enterprise leak benchmark with PII, PHI, and IP marks. Findings indicate that the multi-agent pipeline outperforms the single-agent and rule-based baselines by far in terms of retrieval accuracy, summarization fidelity and privacy protection. In particular, Sensitive Exposure Rate (SER) decreased to 3 percent in comparison with 8-11 percent in other systems, and the rate of hallucination and compliance error also decreased. These conclusions underscore the theoretical usefulness of role-specialized orchestration to enhance an interpretability, controllability, and auditability in pipeline piping with LLM. In practice, the framework is an addition to enterprise governance in that it is a scalable and compliance-based approach to automated leak triage. In addition, it proposes redaction-conscious assessment approach and recommends a way forward along the multi-agent LLMs to multimodal leak management and distributed governance models, responding to the present enterprise needs as well as future regulatory requirements.</jats:p>
title: Multi-agent LLMs for Intelligent Retrieval and Summarization in Enterprise Data Leaks
